Pathology of the Heart II Ischemic Heart Disease and Hypertensive Heart Disease · LE 2 Trans 5B · Dr. Socorro Cruz-Yañez

Whole-Lesson Summary

  • This lecture covers two of the major types of heart disease: Ischemic Heart Disease (IHD) and Hypertensive Heart Disease (HHD), after a brief orientation to all types of heart disease (congenital, ischemic, hypertensive, valvular, non-ischemic myocardial, cardiac neoplasms).
  • IHD = group of related cardiac diseases from an imbalance between blood supply to the heart (perfusion) and its demand for oxygen.
    • In more than 90% of cases the cause is obstructive coronary artery atherosclerotic lesions.
  • IHD has 4 syndromes: Angina Pectoris (ischemia that falls short of infarction), Acute Myocardial Infarction (irreversible cell death, coagulative necrosis), Chronic IHD (progressive CHF from accumulated ischemic damage) and Sudden Cardiac Death (fatal arrhythmia).
  • The AMI story is built on acute plaque change → thrombosis → occlusion → wavefront necrosis, with a predictable morphologic timeline that lets the pathologist estimate the time of infarction.
  • HHD = pressure overload and ventricular hypertrophy from hypertension.
    • Systemic (left-sided) HHD gives concentric LV hypertrophy (>2.0 cm).
    • Pulmonary (right-sided) HHD = cor pulmonale: RV dilatation when acute, RV hypertrophy when chronic.

Main Framework

  • Ischemic Heart Disease (supply–demand imbalance, >90% coronary atherosclerosis)
    • Angina Pectoris: Stable (75% obstruction, exertional, <15 min) · Prinzmetal (vasospasm, at rest) · Unstable (acute plaque change + partial thrombus, >20 min, pre-infarction)
    • Acute MI: Transmural/STEMI (complete occlusive thrombus) vs Subendocardial/NSTEMI (partial occlusion, inner ⅓–½)
    • Chronic IHD ("Ischemic Cardiomyopathy"): cardiomegaly, LV hypertrophy and dilatation, discrete scars, progressive CHF
    • Sudden Cardiac Death: fatal arrhythmia (ventricular fibrillation or asystole), 80–90% with significant CA atherosclerosis
  • Hypertensive Heart Disease (pressure overload → hypertrophy)
    • Systemic (left-sided): concentric LV hypertrophy >2.0 cm + history or evidence of HPN
    • Pulmonary (right-sided, cor pulmonale): Acute → RV dilatation without hypertrophy · Chronic → RV hypertrophy (up to 1.0 cm or more, normal 0.5 cm)

Most Important Must-Know Concepts

Must Know (red-exclamation points in the lecture)
  • TIP: All of the letter Ts in CHD are Right to Left Shunt anomalies.
  • Ischemic episodes in angina pectoris DO NOT produce irreversible cell death.
  • TAKE NOTE: Pattern of progression of necrosis advances in a wavefront manner.
  • Table 6: salient morphological changes at different time intervals following infarction.
  • Irreversible cell injury occurs 20–40 minutes after the onset of ischemia.
    • Medical intervention should be instituted before this time in order to prevent irreversible cell death.
  • Aerobic metabolism ceases within seconds (early biochemical change).
  • Sarcolemmal membrane damage is the earliest detectable feature of myocyte necrosis (early ultrastructural change).
  • TTC staining: Viable myocardium = pink to red areas.
    • Non-viable myocardium = yellow areas.

Types of Heart Disease p. 1–2

TypeLecture definition
Congenital Heart disease
  • Heart malformations found at birth.
  • Multifactorial causes, both genetic and environmental.
Ischemic Heart diseaseInadequate coronary blood perfusion that could not meet the metabolic demands of the heart.
Hypertensive Heart disease
  • Intrinsic heart disease caused by increased pressure coming from systemic or pulmonary circulation.
  • Two types: Systemic & Pulmonary Hypertension.
Valvular Heart disease
  • Intrinsically involve the valvular apparatus of the heart.
  • Can be congenital or acquired.
  • May produce an obstructive or regurgitant lesion.
Non-ischemic myocardial disease
  • Broad class of heart disease.
    • Involves the myocardium that does not have an underlying etiology of ischemia.
  • Involves the various cardiomyopathy, inflammatory processes & diseases of the pericardium.
Cardiac Neoplasms
  • Tumoral growth involving the heart.
    • Can be benign or malignant.
  • Originating primarily on the site of the heart or secondary involving the heart from a metastatic site elsewhere.

AnomalyDiseasesDirection of shunt
Left to Right Shunt Anomaly
  • ASD – Atrial Septal Defect
  • VSD – Ventricular Septal Defect
  • PDA – Patent Ductus Arteriosus
  • AVSD – Atrioventricular Septal Defect
Blood is shunted from high pressure to low pressure chamber.
Right to Left Shunt Anomaly
  • Tetralogy of Fallot
  • Transposition of Great Vessels
  • Truncus Arteriosus

  • Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return
Blood is shunted from the right side to the left side of the heart, bypassing the pulmonary circulation because of the low blood flow to the lungs (usually presents with cyanosis).
Obstructive Anomaly

  • Pulmonic Stenosis / Atresia
  • Aortic Stenosis / Atresia
—
Must Know · TIPAll of the letter Ts in CHD are the Right to Left Shunt anomalies (Tetralogy of Fallot, Transposition of Great Vessels, Truncus Arteriosus, Tricuspid Atresia, Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return).

Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) p. 1

  • Definition: Abnormal opening in the atrial septum leading to direct communication between left and right atrium (left to right shunt anomaly)
  • Most common CHD that is asymptomatic until adulthood, with symptoms appearing in the 3rd decade
  • Acyanotic at birth
  • 10% of CHD
Type of ASD (Table 2)Features
Secundum ASD (90%)
  • Most common.
  • Defect is located in the fossa ovale (communication found in the fetal circulation, but normally closes after birth – the persistence of this continues to provide a connection between the left to right side of the atrium).
Primum ASD (5%)
  • Defect occurs near the AV valve.
  • Associated with a clefted anterior mitral valve (partial ASD).
Sinus Venosus ASD (5%)
  • Located near the entrance of SVC.
  • Associated with TAPVR (Total anomalous pulmonary venous return).

Clinical Features of ASD

  • Asymptomatic in the first 2 decades
  • Symptoms occur in the 3rd–4th decade of life, due to development of pulmonary HPN
  • S/S: dyspnea, fatigue, edema, palpitations, arrhythmia, shortness of breath, murmur
  • Complications: stroke, pulmonary HPN, Eisenmenger complex

The lecture refers to Trans 15 (Pathology of the Heart III–V) for the rest of congenital heart disease.

Ischemic Heart Disease (IHD) p. 2

Definition Must Know

  • Also called "Coronary Heart Disease" (CHD) or "Coronary Artery Disease" (CAD)
  • Group of related cardiac diseases resulting from imbalance between blood supply to the heart (perfusion) & its demand for oxygen (myocardial ischemia)
  • Broad term encompassing several closely related syndromes caused primarily by myocardial ischemia
    • Imbalance between cardiac blood supply perfusion and myocardial oxygen and nutritional requirements
    • Leads to biochemical, ultrastructural, gross and microscopic alterations related to reversible & irreversible hypoxic injury
  • More than 90% of cases: myocardial ischemia results from reduced blood flow due to an obstructive coronary artery atherosclerotic lesion

Heart is susceptible to hypoxic injury

  • 20 minute loss of oxygen supply to the heart muscle will induce irreversible damage
  • Cardiac ischemia is less tolerated in comparison to ischemia of skeletal muscles, skin, bones & soft tissues

Disease progression

  • Insidious, slow progressing process, spanning several decades of life
  • Often times silent and asymptomatic initially before sudden onset of symptoms
  • Late manifestation of coronary atherosclerosis that began during childhood or adolescence and progress to significant, critical level of coronary occlusion

Syndromes of IHD p. 2

SyndromeLecture descriptionKey anchor
Acute Myocardial InfarctionPresence of an occlusion or precipitous reduction of the coronary blood flow resulting to ischemia with irreversible cell deathPattern of cell death: Coagulative Necrosis
Angina Pectoris
  • Various degree of chest or precordial pain due to reduction of coronary perfusion.
  • Reduction of perfusion falls short of ischemia and cell death
Clinical importance: may foretell the development of a more serious myocardial infarction
Chronic Ischemic Heart DiseaseInsidious, slow growing & progressive deterioration of heart function due to repeated bouts of subclinical ischemia of cardiac myocytes that results to fibrosis of the myocardium & atrophy of the heart
  • 90% associated with significant occluding CA atherosclerosis.
  • Presents with insidious onset of congestive heart failure
Sudden Cardiac DeathSudden death within 24 hours or an hour from the onset of symptomsUnderlying: fatal arrhythmias with accompanying significant CA atherosclerosis

Risk Factors p. 2

  • The same risk factors with atherosclerosis
    • 90% of cases of IHD have underlying coronary artery atherosclerosis
    • Patients with these risk factors have 3–5 times the risk of developing IHD & AMI in comparison to the general population
Modifiable Risk Factors (Table 3)Non-modifiable (Fixed) Risk Factors
  • Diet, Hyperlipidemia
  • HPN and DM
  • Cigarette Smoking
  • Age, Gender
  • Familial predisposition

Newer Risk Factors in IHD

  • Inflammatory: CRP, Ferritin, leukocyte count
  • Thrombotic: Fibrinogen, inherited polymorphism
  • Other lipids: Lpa, ApoE polymorphism
  • Homocysteine
  • Others: Anti-oxidants, Resveratrol

Epidemiology (core points only)

  • IHD causes more death and disability and incurs greater economic costs than any other illness in the developed world.
    • Single largest cause of mortality worldwide.
  • Peak incidence: Males over 60 years old, Females over 70 years old.
    • Men are more commonly affected than women.
  • Incidence typically starts at the 4th decade of life and increases with age
  • Primary pathologic process that leads to IHD is atherosclerosis
  • More than 70% of at-risk individuals have multiple risk factors.
    • Only 2–7% of the general population have no risk factors.

Etiology: Supply and Demand p. 3

  • Myocardial supply and demand is a key concept in understanding the pathophysiology of myocardial ischemia
  • Normal physiology:
    • For any given level of demand for oxygen → myocardium will control level of oxygen → prevent underperfusion of myocytes and subsequent development of ischemia and infarction
    • When oxygen demand is high, the heart adapts by improving heart rate, force of contraction, and myocardial wall tension
  • Ischemic heart disease: relative disparity between the supply of oxygen and the need for oxygen by the cardiac myocytes, caused by reduced coronary blood perfusion relative to blood demand

Underlying causes of reduction of coronary blood flow

  • Fixed stenosing atherosclerosis
    • Critical stenosis is 70% lumen stenosis
  • Fissure, rupture, ulceration, and hemorrhage due to acute plaque change
    • Critical in the development of progression to acute myocardial infarction
  • CA thrombosis
  • CA vasoconstriction or vasospasm
  • CA emboli, CA vasculitis
  • Mild to moderate degree of CA occlusions may become aggravated in the setting of increased cardiac energy demand (e.g. myocardial hypertrophy, increased physical activity, exercise, or increased heart rate), hypoxemia
  • Can be mitigated by the presence of hypoxemia and hypotension

Pathogenesis: Degree of Stenosis p. 3

  • More than 90% of patients with IHD have coexisting CA atherosclerosis
    • Involves 1 or more coronary arteries, often referred to as multi-vessel involvement
    • Most important underlying cause of coronary artery obstruction
Degree of obstructionConsequence (lecture wording)
Critical stenosis at 70%
  • 70% obstruction of the cross sectional area of the blood vessel → effort related ischemia, insufficient CA vasodilation
  • Onset of symptoms occur at critical stenosis
  • CA vasodilation is insufficient in meeting myocardial demand
90% CA obstruction
  • → ischemia at rest
  • Symptoms are present even at rest
  • Significant reduction of coronary blood flow
Slowly developing occlusionCollateral formation: slow developing CA obstruction → formation of alternate collateral vessels → can improve perfusion of myocardium
Important Values
  • 20 minutes loss of oxygen → irreversible damage.
  • 70% lumen stenosis = critical stenosis → effort-related ischemia.
  • 90% obstruction → ischemia at rest.
  • >90% of IHD has coexisting CA atherosclerosis.

Role of Fixed Coronary Obstruction p. 3

  • Definition: Type of coronary artery narrowing caused by a stable atherosclerotic plaque deposited in the tunica intima
  • Growth: Slowly growing plaques expand gradually due to accumulation of lipid in foam cells and migration and proliferation of smooth muscle cell in the intima
    • Plaques tend to stabilize, and are not prone to rupture
    • Resultant atheroma consists of a fibro-fatty plaque, covered usually by a thick fibrous cap that shows no superimposed acute complicated lesions like ulcerations, hemorrhage, fissures, or cracks
  • 90% of CA narrowing is due to fixed CA atherosclerosis
    • Produces a chronic, progressive, obstruction of the blood flow, oftentimes without symptoms, and accompanied by formation of alternate coronary collateral channels
  • Vessels: May affect single, dual, or triple coronary arteries commonly involved simultaneously: Left anterior descending, Left circumflex, Right coronary artery
    • Atherosclerotic deposits in small penetrating coronary arteries that serve the deep myocardium are rare
  • S/S dependent on extent, severity of occlusion, and acute plaque change
  • Associated with typical angina pectoris

Role of Acute Plaque Change p. 3–4

  • Occurs when a fixed coronary artery atheroma undergoes abrupt plaque changes such as: Rupture, Fissuring, Superficial Erosion, Ulceration, Hemorrhage
  • Ischemia precipitated by acute plaque changes predisposed to thrombus formation through platelet aggregation
    • Thrombus will further aggravate pre-existing occlusion and luminal narrowing leading to partial or complete occlusion
    • This results to a sudden decrease in coronary blood flow leading to acute coronary syndrome

Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) Must Know

  • A spectrum of clinical conditions associated with sudden reduced coronary blood flow:
    • Unstable angina pectoris
    • Acute myocardial infarction
    • Sudden cardiac death
  • Associated with the sudden conversion of a stable atherosclerotic plaque to an unstable and potentially life-threatening atherothrombotic lesion initiated by acute plaque changes

Role of Thrombosis p. 4

  • Significant role in the pathogenesis of IHD
    • Coronary arteries with acute plaque change can predispose the formation of non-occlusive thrombus
    • Acute, sudden instability and change in atheroma will precipitate formation of platelet aggregates forming a primary hemostatic plug with conversion to a more stable hemostatic plug through the contribution of clotting factors
  • Thrombosis builds up a thrombus which may propagate and cause partial or complete CA occlusion
  • Causes myocardial ischemia resulting in acute coronary syndromes (ACS)
Thrombus typeAssociated with
Complete occlusive thrombusAcute transmural myocardial infarction
Partial occlusive thrombusPatients with pre-infarction or unstable angina pectoris, subendocardial infarction, and sudden cardiac death

Non-Atheromatous Coronary Arterial Occlusion p. 4

  • Occurs in <10% of cases (90% are caused by atheromatous plaque)
  • Causes:
    • CA Embolism: usually of the cholesterol type
    • Dissecting aneurysm: involves root of aorta, secondary occlusion of coronary ostia by dissecting hematoma
    • CA Vasospasm
    • Congenital anomalies of coronary vessels
    • Trauma
    • Vasculitis/inflammation: seen in Kawasaki's vasculitis.
      • Can damage the vascular endothelium which can predispose to formation of a thrombus

Role of Vasoconstriction p. 4

  • Reduction of lumen size and diameter
Vasoconstriction→reduce CA blood flow→ischemia
Vasoconstriction→increases local mechanical forces→increase risk of plaque rupture
  • Plays a role in the pathogenesis of acute plaque change
  • The vasoreactive CA can undergo vasoconstriction and can be stimulated by:
    • Adrenergic agents or sympathetic agents
    • Platelet factors release during endothelial injury with the formation of platelet aggregates
    • Endothelial secretions (principally mediated by endothelin)

Role of Inflammation p. 4

  • Causes of inflammation can range from various infectious agents, chemical, and physical exposures
  • Mechanism involves damage to the intima resulting in the formation of an initial lesion
    • Initial lesion: interaction between endothelial cells & circulating leukocytes leading to the accumulation of T cells & macrophages, producing cytokines (TNF, IL-6, and IFN-gamma) similar to the pathway of the inflammatory responses
    • Later stages: secretion of metalloproteinase by macrophages
  • Diagnostic marker: Elevated C-reactive Protein (CRP), important for diagnosis of inflammation
High-Yield Recap · The 5 mechanisms of IHD
  • Fixed obstruction (stable plaque, thick fibrous cap, 90% of narrowing) → typical angina.
  • Acute plaque change (rupture, fissuring, erosion, ulceration, hemorrhage) → ACS.
  • Thrombosis: complete → transmural MI, partial → unstable angina, subendocardial MI, SCD.
  • Vasoconstriction: adrenergic agents, platelet factors, endothelin.
  • Inflammation: T cells, macrophages, TNF, IL-6, IFN-gamma, metalloproteinase, elevated CRP.

Angina Pectoris (AP) p. 5

Definition Must Know

  • Paroxysmal, usually recurrent attacks of precordial or substernal chest pain, or discomfort caused by transient (usually lasting for 15 seconds to minutes episodes) myocardial ischemia which falls short of infarction
    • This ischemia is insufficient to induce myocardial necrosis
  • 3 types:
    • Stable or typical AP (classical): most common form
    • Prinzmetal or variant AP
    • Unstable or pre-infarction AP (crescendo AP)
Must KnowIschemic episodes in angina pectoris DO NOT produce irreversible cell death.

Case Scenario (Stable AP) p. 5

52/M, a CFO of a multinational company complains of sudden onset of substernal chest pain with radiation to the left arm. The pain occurred as he was running late for a meeting. The pain was described as mild, burning-like pain, lasting for 2 min without any other symptoms. The pain subsided after resting while sitting down.

  • Key features: Age/Sex/Risk Occupation: 52/M, CFO.
    • Acute transient, evanescent mild chest pain with radiation to left arm, pain related to exertion, relieved by rest.
  • The referred pain corresponds to the dermatomal level of the heart during embryogenesis
  • This typical clinical presentation is the classical presentation of the pain of Angina Pectoris

Etiology of Angina p. 5

  • Anginal pain is a consequence of ischemia-induced release of adenosine, bradykinin and other molecules that stimulate the sympathetic and vagal afferent nerves
  • Caused by varying combinations of increased myocardial demand and decreased myocardial perfusion and coronary arterial pathology secondary to:
    • Chronic stenosing coronary atherosclerosis
    • Disrupted atherosclerotic plaques
    • Coronary artery vasospasm
    • In-situ thrombosis occlusive in nature in the CAs
    • Coronary artery embolization

Stable Angina Pectoris p. 5

  • Most common form of AP.
    • "Typical or Classical Angina Pectoris"
  • Usually 75% CA obstruction
  • Reduction of perfusion caused by chronic stenosing CA atherosclerosis and inappropriate CA vasoconstriction
  • Clinical presentation:
    • Intermittent and transient (< 15 mins)
    • Precipitated by physical exertion and emotion
    • Relieved by rest and vasodilators
  • Etiology:
    • With the progressive narrowing of the lumen, adequate blood flow is prevented from reaching the myocardium resulting in a mismatch between cardiac oxygen demand and cardiac blood flow perfusion.
      • Aggravated by physical or emotional exertion.
    • Presence of atherosclerotic plaques may also induce episodes of inappropriate CA vasoconstriction resulting in further CA narrowing
    • Mild, rapidly reversible brief episodes of myocardial ischemia
  • Summary: Fairly predictable intermittent episodes of brief, transient precordial pain precipitated by physical and emotional exertion

Prinzmetal Angina Pectoris p. 5

  • "Variant Angina Pectoris".
    • Uncommon form
  • Episodic pain at rest and is not effort or emotion related (unlike Stable AP)
    • Secondary to sudden and inappropriate CA vasospasm
  • More common in younger patients with fewer cardiovascular risk factors
  • Etiology (not well understood):
    • CA vasospasm occurs in segments that appear to be healthy.
      • Mechanism leading to intense vasospasm is thought to involve increased sympathetic activity in combination with endothelial dysfunction
    • CA atherosclerosis may induce vasospasm in inappropriately sensitive segments of the coronary artery, reducing coronary blood flow to the point that it cannot meet the cardiac demand for oxygen → transient myocardial ischemia
    • Episodes are brief and reversible and the CA vasospasm does NOT lead to a more serious myocardial infarction or irreversible cell death
  • Clinical features:
    • Episodes of transient anginal chest pain that can occur at rest
    • May be associated with a temporary ST segment elevation in ECG
    • Responds well to nitroglycerin, calcium channel blockers, and vasodilators

Unstable Angina Pectoris p. 5–6

  • "Pre-infarction", "Crescendo", or "Q-wave" Angina Pectoris
  • Pattern of increasingly frequent and more prolonged lasting (> 20 mins) severe chest or precordial pain
  • Precipitated by progressively lower levels of physical activity and may even occur at rest
  • Acceleration of symptoms of stable angina pectoris
  • Associated with acute plaque change with superimposed partial thrombosis and vasospasm
  • Has at least one of these features:
    • Occurs at rest or in minimal exertion usually lasting more than 20 mins
    • Severe and new onset
    • Occurs in a crescendo pattern: more severe, progressive, prolonged or more frequent than before
  • Precursor to the development of an acute myocardial infarction, hence called "pre-infarction angina pectoris"
  • Underlying pathophysiologic mechanism:
    • Acute plaque destruction
    • Transient platelet aggregation with the formation of a partial thrombus with significant coronary artery reduction of the blood flow
    • Coronary artery vasospasm can also occur, producing and progressing to complete vascular occlusion resulting in ischemia and infarction

Comparison of the 3 Types of Angina

FeatureStable (Typical)Prinzmetal (Variant)Unstable (Pre-infarction, Crescendo)
FrequencyMost commonUncommon—
MechanismChronic stenosing CA atherosclerosis (usually 75% obstruction) + inappropriate vasoconstrictionSudden, inappropriate CA vasospasm (increased sympathetic activity + endothelial dysfunction)Acute plaque change + superimposed partial thrombosis and vasospasm
TriggerPhysical exertion and emotionAt rest, not effort or emotion relatedProgressively lower levels of activity, may occur at rest
Duration< 15 mins, intermittent and transientBrief and reversible> 20 mins, more prolonged and frequent
ECG—Temporary ST segment elevation"Q-wave" angina
ReliefRest and vasodilatorsNitroglycerin, calcium channel blockers, vasodilators—
Patient—Younger, fewer CV risk factors—
SignificanceMild, rapidly reversible ischemiaDoes NOT lead to MI or irreversible cell deathPrecursor of acute MI
Key Differentiator
  • Exertion-related and relieved by rest → Stable AP.
  • At rest in a young patient with ST elevation that responds to vasodilators → Prinzmetal AP.
  • Crescendo pattern, >20 min, new onset or at rest → Unstable AP (pre-infarction).

Case Scenario: Progression to AMI p. 6

Same 52/M, a CFO, complains of sudden crushing, severe substernal chest pain during a board meeting with diaphoresis and light headedness. He took his sublingual medications, but the pain persisted. ECG showed ST segment elevation. BP was 100/60 (usual BP is 150/90), HR of 110/min and RR of 24/min. Troponin T and Troponin I levels were increased.

  • Risk factors: 52/M, works as a Chief Financial Officer (CFO), stress
  • Acute, crushing, severe substernal chest pain with diaphoresis and light headedness
  • No relief with nitroglycerins
  • PE: mild hypotension (100/60 mmHg), HR 110/min (tachycardia), RR 24/min (tachypnea)
  • Diagnosis: ECG – ST segment elevation.
    • Increased Troponin T and Troponin I (cardiac markers of injury)
Clinical CueIf you see angina pain that persists despite sublingual medication, with ST elevation and raised troponins → think Acute Myocardial Infarction, not angina.

Myocardial Infarction (MI) p. 6

Definition Must Know

  • a.k.a. heart attack
  • Localized area of cardiac muscle necrosis due to ischemia
    • Irreversible necrosis of heart muscle secondary to prolonged ischemia
    • Results from an imbalance in oxygen supply and demand usually due to a CA atherosclerosis with plaque rupture and superimposed occlusive thrombus
    • Leads to sudden reduction of blood supply to a portion of the myocardium

Epidemiology and Risk Factors (core points)

  • Leading cause of death in developed nations, seen in 5–12% of autopsies
  • More common in males over 45 years old.
    • Equal in incidence with post-menopausal women (decline in cardioprotection due to estrogen levels)
  • Risk factors similar to atherosclerosis because 90% of patients with IHD and AMI have concomitant CA atherosclerosis
Major (Table 4)Non-modifiable (Fixed) Risk Factors
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • HPN
  • DM
  • Cigarette Smoking
  • Obesity
  • Age & Sex
  • Stress
  • Physical inactivity

Pathogenesis of AMI p. 6

  • Sudden precipitous reduction of coronary artery perfusion
  • Coronary artery obstruction and occlusion
    • Atherosclerosis undergoing acute plaque change with development of an occlusive thrombus with vasospasm
    • Major mechanism of AMI
  • Increase myocardial demand: myocardial requirement for oxygen is high (e.g. severe anemia).
    • Coronary artery perfusion is compromised due to preexisting coronary artery disease or abnormality
  • Hemodynamic compromise: shock states which reduce oxygen content in blood and induce inadequate perfusion of myocardium
  • Emboli: usually cholesterol type which can be dislodged from another site and become impacted in the coronary artery and produce sudden occlusion
  • Vasculitis (e.g. Kawasaki's)
  • Unknown (idiopathic)

Sequence of Coronary Artery Thrombosis p. 6

1Fixed atheromatous plaque undergoes acute plaque change (fissure, ulcer, hemorrhage)
Initiating event: plaque becomes eroded or suddenly disrupted by endothelial injury, intraplaque hemorrhage, or mechanical forces that exposes the subendothelial collagen and necrotic plaque contents to the blood
↓
2Platelets adhere, aggregate, forming primary hemostatic plug and induce vasospasm
Activated platelets release thromboxane, adenosine diphosphate, and serotonin, causing further platelet aggregation and secondary CA vasospasm
↓
3Tissue factor activates coagulation pathway
Activation of clotting factors by extrinsic and intrinsic pathways which further stabilizes the clot
↓
4Thrombus propagates and occludes lumen leading to infarction
Thrombus is generated within minutes. When the CA becomes completely occluded → ischemia and irreversible death producing necrosis of cardiac myocytes
Must Know · Pattern of cell deathCoagulative necrosis is the typical type of cell death in AMI.

Myocardial Changes in AMI: Wavefront Progression p. 7

  • Coagulation necrosis follows 20–40 minutes of ischemia
  • Initially at subendocardial region with wavefront progression
    • Irreversible injury of ischemic myocytes starts at the subendocardial zone
    • This is the least perfused region in the myocardium and thus vulnerable to hypoxemia
    • Exposed to relatively high intramural pressure which acts to impede the inflow of blood
    • With more prolonged ischemia, a wavefront direction of cell death progresses, extending and enlarging the size of ischemic injury
    • Cell death moves through other regions of the myocardium driven by progressive tissue edema, myocardial-derived reactive oxygen species, and inflammatory mediators
  • Morphologic changes evolve over time: the changes post-infarction show the characteristic temporal evolution
Must Know · TAKE NOTEPattern of progression of necrosis advances in a wavefront manner.

Pathologic Forms of MI (Table 5) p. 7–8

FeatureTransmural InfarctionSub-endocardial Infarction
ExtentFull thickness of the coagulative necrosis of the ventricular wallInner 1/3 to half of ventricular wall – only involves a small area of the subendocardium
CauseResult of a complete thrombotic occlusion of the coronary artery with underlying atherosclerosis
  • Caused by partial occlusion of the coronary artery without an acute plaque change.
  • Decreased circulating blood volume (shock, hypotension, partial CA occlusion or vasospasm)
ECGSTEMI (ST Elevation Myocardial Infarct) because of the characteristic ECG changes of the ST segmentNSTEMI (Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarct) because of the absence of significant ST segment elevation
Other namea.k.a. Systemic Type of AMI—
AssociationChronic atherosclerotic obstruction, acute plaque change, and superimposed complete thrombosisDiffuse stenosing CA atherosclerosis without thrombosis and acute plaque change
Do Not Confuse
  • Transmural = STEMI = complete occlusive thrombus = full thickness.
  • Subendocardial = NSTEMI = partial occlusion, no acute plaque change = inner ⅓ to ½.

Myocardial Changes in AMI p. 8

Biochemical changes

  • Anaerobic glycolysis
    • Must Know Aerobic metabolism ceases within seconds (early biochemical change)
    • Leads to inadequate production of high energy phosphates like ATP and accumulation of potentially noxious metabolites like lactic acids
  • ATP, creatine phosphate reduction
  • Lactic acidosis

Ultrastructural changes

  • Cell and mitochondrial swelling: within minutes at the onset following ischemia
  • Myofibrillar relaxation
  • Glycogen depletion
  • Sarcolemmal membrane damage
    • Must Know Earliest detectable feature of myocyte necrosis (early ultrastructural change)
    • Allows intracellular macromolecules to leak out of the necrotic cells into the cardiac interstitium → microvasculature → lymphatics
    • Escape of intracellular myocardial proteins into the circulation forms the basis for blood tests that can sensitively detect irreversible myocyte damage
    • Cardiac enzymes like troponin, CPK-MB, LDH are elevated and used as ancillary tests in the diagnosis and management of AMI

Approximate Time of Onset of Key Events (Table 7) p. 8

FeatureTime
Onset of ATP depletionSeconds
Loss of contractility<2 minutes
ATP reduced to 50% of normal10 minutes
ATP reduced to 10% of normal40 minutes
Irreversible cell injury Must Know20–40 minutes
Microvascular injury>1 hour
  • ATP is needed for:
    • Generation of energy-dependent ATP pumps across the membrane
    • Maintenance of the organelle cellular membrane and nuclear membrane integrity
  • Irreversible cell injury occurs 20 to 40 minutes after the onset of ischemia
Must KnowMedical intervention should be instituted before this time (20–40 minutes) in order to prevent irreversible cell death.

Irreversible Myocardial Damage p. 8

  • Following severe ischemia lasting from 20–40 minutes or longer, and affects initially the subendocardial region
  • Wavefront spread of necrosis moves through other regions of the myocardium, driven by:
    • Progressive tissue edema
    • Myocardial-derived ROS
    • Inflammatory mediators
  • Initial damage to the sarcolemmal membrane

AMI Morphology: Early Recognition with TTC p. 8

  • Early Recognition: use of Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) (unstained area)
    • TTC is a substrate for lactic dehydrogenase (LDH)
    • LDH transforms TTC from a yellow substance to a formazan salt, which is deep purple in color
    • Useful to detect the status of myocardium areas
    • Very sensitive technique: detects AMI as early as 30 mins post-infarction when the dead myocytes start leaking LDH into the bloodstream and do not change TTC into formazan salt
Must Know · TTC colors
  • Viable myocardium: pink to red areas.
  • Non-viable myocardium: yellow areas.
Exam TrapThe infarct is the area that does NOT stain (yellow). Dead myocytes have leaked out their LDH, so there is no enzyme left to turn TTC purple.

Morphologic Evolution of AMI p. 8

  • The morphologic changes of AMI are predictable.
    • They undergo a series of evolving morphologic changes and these are important in estimating the time of infarction.
Must Know · Table 6 (with Tables 8 and 9, as combined in the Appendix)Salient morphological changes at different time intervals following infarction. The full table is below. Learn each row.
StageTimeGross FeaturesLight MicroscopeElectron Microscope
Reversible Injury0–½ hrNoneNone
  • Relaxation of myofibrils
  • Glycogen loss
  • Mitochondrial swelling
Irreversible Injury½–4 hrNone
  • Usually none
  • Variable waviness of fibers at border
  • Sarcolemmal disruption
  • Mitochondrial amorphous densities
4–12 hrOccasionally dark mottling
  • Beginning coagulation necrosis
  • Edema
  • Hemorrhage
—
12–24 hrDark mottling
  • Ongoing coagulation necrosis
  • Pyknosis of nuclei
  • Myocyte hypereosinophilia
  • Marginal contraction band necrosis
  • Beginning neutrophilic infiltrate
—
1–3 daysMottling with a yellow-tan infarct center
  • Coagulation necrosis, with loss of nuclei and striations
  • Interstitial infiltrate of neutrophils
—
3–7 days
  • Hyperemic border
  • Central yellow-tan softening
  • Beginning of disintegration of dead myofibers with dying neutrophils
  • Early phagocytosis of dead cells by macrophages at the infarct border
—
7–10 daysMaximally yellow-tan and soft with depressed red-tan margins
  • Well-developed phagocytosis of dead cells
  • Early formation of fibrovascular granulation tissue at margins
—
10–14 daysRed-gray depressed infarct bordersWell-established granulation tissue with angiogenesis and collagen deposition—

High-Yield Recap · Flow of the timeline
½–4 hr wavy fibers→4–12 hr coagulation necrosis, hemorrhage, edema→12–24 hr hypereosinophilia, contraction bands, few leukocytes, gross mottling→1–3 d neutrophils, tiger stripe→3–7 d macrophages, softening, rupture risk→7–10 d maximally soft, early granulation→10–14 d granulation tissue→2–8 wk fibrous scar→>2 mo dense scar

30 Minutes to 4 Hours: Wavy and Thinned Fibers p. 9

  • Wavy and thinned myocardial fibers are the earliest light microscopic changes seen in AMI
    • Induced by the increased hydrostatic pressure of interstitial edema, which squeezes and stretches the neighboring fibers
  • Nuclei are not pyknotic and show no karyolysis, with mild interstitial edema surrounding the wavy fibers
    • Thinner in diameter in comparison to the adjacent non-wavy cardiac myocytes
    • Distinct lack of polymorphonuclear leukocyte infiltration
    • Thinned wavy fibers appear hypereosinophilic with contraction bands

Contraction Band Necrosis

  • Seen in conjunction with wavy fibers in AMI
  • Shows transverse hypereosinophilic bands alternating with pale granular spaces along the length of myocytes
    • Transverse bands are due to the overlapping hypercontracted sarcomeres

4 to 12 Hours: Coagulation Necrosis, Hemorrhage, Edema p. 9

  • Coagulation necrosis seen within the cardiac muscles
    • Showing various forms of nuclear death: Karyopyknosis, Karyolysis, and dissolution and loss of nuclei
    • Hypereosinophilic coagulated cytoplasm surrounded by areas of edema and hemorrhages
    • Necrotic heart muscles still maintain their ghost outlines, although without cellular details

12 to 24 Hours: Myocyte Hypereosinophilia, Contraction Band, Few Leukocytes p. 9–10

  • The gross findings of an infarct become visible at 12–24 hours post-infarction
  • The infarcted heart becomes dark red and soft with a mottling effect reflecting the accompanying vascular congestion and hemorrhages
  • Coagulation necrosis becomes more apparent on gross and microscopic levels in 24 hours of infarction

1 to 3 Days: Mottling, Dark, and Yellow Areas (Tiger Stripe) p. 10

  • Gross: Papillary muscles exhibit the characteristic "Tiger Stripe Appearance"
    • Caused by alternating pale yellow infarcted areas with dark red hemorrhagic areas, which produces the mottled gross appearance
  • Microscopic: coagulation necrosis with hyper-eosinophilic cytoplasm, ongoing loss of cellular detail (karyolysis with loss of nuclei and loss of cross striations), accompanied by a prominent and increasing number of leukocytic inflammatory infiltrations
  • Necrotic cardiomyocytes show pink, coagulated proteins within dead muscles with preservation of the cell outlines of ghost and dead cells (Figure 21)

3 to 7 Days p. 10

  • Gross: Central yellow tan softening and depression of infarcted muscle surrounded by red hyperemic borders
  • Microscopic: disintegration of dead myocytes and accompanying leukocytes, early phagocytosis of dead cells by macrophages
Exam Trap · Lecturer emphasisAt this point in time where the heart muscles are maximally soft, this is when the heart is liable to rupture. It undergoes left ventricular rupture and hemopericardium is the complication.

10 to 14 Days p. 11

  • Gross: Red-Gray Depressed Center.
    • Pale areas represent old scarred myocardial infarction
  • Microscopic: Well-developed Granulation Tissue
    • Necrotic cardiac myocytes have been largely phagocytized and replaced by healing granulation tissue made up of collagen
    • Few lymphocytes, histiocytes, and formed blood vessels
    • Ingrowth of fibrous connective tissue with phagocytosis and development of a granulation type of healing inflammation at the border of the infarction

2 to 8 Weeks: Fibrous Scar Replacing Necrotic Heart Muscles p. 11

  • Gross: Red infarcted areas of earlier lesions have been replaced with white and pale well-developed fibrous scar tissue
  • Microscopic:
    • Replacement fibrosis of dead myocytes
    • Scars and fibrous tissue consist of poorly cellular, hyalinized collagen fibers
    • Inflammatory cells wane over time and may be absent

Clinical Features of AMI p. 11

3 important parameters for diagnosing AMI Must Know

  • Classical clinical presentation of S/S: severe chest pain, rapid, weak pulse, diaphoresis, dyspnea, nausea, vomiting
  • Diagnostic changes in EKG/ECG: ST segment elevation, new Q waves
  • Laboratory markers of cardiac cell injury: CPK-MB, cardiac troponins I & T (TropI, TropT), Creatine Kinase, LDH, CRP
    • Absence of a change in the levels of CK and CK-MB during the first 2 days of chest pain & of troponin in the days following essentially excludes the diagnosis of MI

Classical vs Atypical Clinical Presentation p. 11–12

Classical Clinical Presentation

  • Prolonged (>30 minutes) chest pain described as "crushing, stabbing, or squeezing" that may radiate to the left arm, back, neck, or jaw
    • Felt as "if a ton of bricks is piled on top of their chest"
    • Patients would typically bend forward and clutch their chest with their fist
  • Rapid (tachycardia) and weak pulse
  • Diaphoresis (profuse sweating)
  • Dyspnea (shortness of breath)
  • Dizziness, nausea & vomiting

Atypical Clinical Presentation

  • May be present among diabetics and females
  • Diabetics: may be asymptomatic due to the presence of peripheral neuropathy
  • Women: chest pain, but may be lesser in degree and intensity with aberrant locations (neck pain, back pain, epigastric pain), which may make diagnosis difficult

EKG/ECG Presentation p. 12

  • Characteristic ECG changes: ST segment elevation, New Q waves
TypeECGInfarct typeOcclusionSeverity
STEMI (ST-elevation MI)Presence of ST-segment elevationTransmural infarctionComplete thrombotic occlusion of the coronary arteryMore serious form
NSTEMI (Non-ST Elevation MI)Absence of ST-segment elevationSubendocardial infarctionPartial thrombotic occlusionLess serious form

Laboratory Test (Blood): Cardiac Markers of Injury p. 12

  • Used in diagnosing and monitoring the extent & magnitude of infarction
  • Based on the measurement of blood levels of proteins that leak out of the irreversibly damaged cardiac myocytes

CK-MB

  • Isomer of creatine kinase
  • 3 Types of Creatine Kinase:
    • CK-BB: main source is from the brain
    • CK-MB: an intermediate moving CK found mainly in the heart muscles
    • CK-MM: slowest moving CK found mainly in skeletal muscle
  • During Acute MI: Elevated by 4–8 hours post-infarct · Peak at 18 hours · Return to normal 2–3 days

Cardiac Troponins I & T (TropI, TropT) Must Know

  • Most clinically useful biomarkers of myocardial damage due to its high sensitivity and specificity
  • Normally, they are regulatory proteins of calcium-mediated contraction of cardiac muscles
  • During Acute MI: Elevated troponin blood levels (beyond threshold) · Elevated by 2–4 hours · Peak at 24–48 hours · Return to normal 7–10 days
  • Significant troponin elevation is also seen in other conditions that cause death of cardiac myocytes (e.g. myocarditis, myocardial trauma)
  • Low levels of serum troponin elevation ("troponin leak") can occur in other conditions (e.g. CHF, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, and iatrogenic causes from cardiac resuscitation measures)

LDH

  • During Acute MI: Elevated by 24 hours post-infarct (Table 10 lists 2–4 hrs) · Peaks by 3–6 hours · Return to normal 8–14 days
  • Lacks analytical specificity since non-cardiac conditions can produce its elevation (e.g. shock states, RBC hemolysis, carcinomatosis)

Serum Markers Used to Diagnose MI (Table 10) p. 12

MarkerElevated byPeakReturns to Normal
CK-MB4–8 hrs18 hrs2–3 days
Troponin I & T2–4 hrs24–48 hrs7–10 days
LDH2–4 hrs3–6 hrs8–14 days
Lecture-Specific NoteThe lecture text gives LDH "elevated by 24 hours" while Table 10 lists "2–4 hrs". Both values are in the trans. Table 10 is the lecturer's PPT table.
Key Differentiator
  • Troponin = most sensitive and specific, longest to normalize (7–10 days).
  • CK-MB = heart-muscle CK isomer, peaks at 18 hrs, normalizes fastest (2–3 days).
  • LDH = non-specific (hemolysis, shock), normalizes last (8–14 days).

Factors Affecting Severity of AMI p. 12–13

FactorLecture points
Location and severity of obstruction
  • Usually involves the left ventricle (right ventricle and both atria normally spared).
  • Occlusion of the anterior descending branch, supplying the interventricular septum, is often associated with a potentially fatal arrhythmia.
  • 90% occlusion is more likely to produce ischemia and infarction as compared to occlusion of only 35–50% of the lumen.
Rate of development of occlusion
  • Faster rate of development of occlusion → higher probability of ischemia and necrosis.
  • In a rapidly developing occlusion, there is no time to form alternative collateral circulation → infarction.
Size of infarct
  • Occlusion of a main branch of the left circumflex (LCX) or left anterior descending (LAD) can potentially produce a wider area of ischemic necrosis, in contrast to occlusion of small penetrating arterioles supplying the subendocardial region.
  • Right ventricle is affected by right coronary artery (RCA) occlusions, leading to posterior septal or left ventricular infarction.
    • Right sided HF is a common outcome.
Duration of occlusion
  • Longer duration → higher probability of irreversible ischemic injury.
  • Ischemia lasting >20 mins = irreversible damage.
Extent of collateral vessels
  • May spell the difference whether infarction will happen or not.
  • Collateral vessels provide alternative vascular supply when a vessel is occluded.
Metabolic oxygen demands of myocardiumSevere hypertrophic heart → higher levels of metabolic demand as compared to a normal heart.
Other factors
  • BP, HR, cardiac rhythm, blood oxygenation can affect severity of AMI.
  • Anemia and presence of comorbidities undermine cardiovascular status and increase the risk and severity of ischemia.

Complications of Myocardial Infarction p. 13

  • About ¾ of patients experience one or more complications
  • No Complication / Uncomplicated MI (10–20% of cases): patients come in with just pain with no other signs related to complications
ComplicationFrequencyKey lecture points
Contractile DysfunctionMost frequent clinical complication (60%)
  • Heart Failure (60%), Cardiogenic Shock (10%).
  • Risk of contractile dysfunction and heart failure is proportional to size and magnitude of infarction.
  • Left Ventricular Failure (LVF) may manifest as hypotension, pulmonary edema, and congestion.
  • Severe Pump Failure/Cardiogenic Shock: roughly 10% of patients with transmural MI, associated with infarcts that damage 40% or more of the left ventricle.
Papillary Muscle DysfunctionRare
  • Infarction can induce papillary muscle contractile dysfunction or worse, papillary muscle rupture.
  • Fibrosis and scarring post-infarct can shorten and retract the papillary muscle → mitral valve incompetence and regurgitation.
Right Ventricular InfarctionRare (1–3%)
  • From RCA occlusion.
  • Right sided HF is a common outcome.
Myocardial RuptureFatal, 1–5%
  • Can occur in the free wall of the left ventricle, interventricular septum, or papillary muscles.
  • Left ventricular free wall rupture is most common → rapidly fatal hemopericardium and cardiac tamponade.
  • Ventricular septal rupture → acquired ventricular septal defect, left-to-right shunting.
  • Papillary muscle rupture → mitral regurgitation.
  • Occurs most commonly within 3–7 days post-infarct, when the heart is maximally soft due to lysing of necrotic muscles and conversion to granulation tissue.
Arrhythmias, Heart Block & Sudden DeathCommon. 90% develop rhythm disturbance
  • Involves infarcts of the interventricular septum (pathway of electrical impulse conduction).
  • Leads to myocardial irritability and conduction disturbances that can cause sudden cardiac death.
  • Includes heart block, tachyarrhythmia, asystole, bradycardia, premature ventricular contractions.
    • Sometimes fatal ventricular fibrillation.
  • Risk for serious arrhythmias is greatest in the 1st hour post-infarction.
Pericarditis: Local or Autoimmune (Dressler Syndrome)—
  • Complication of a transmural MI eliciting fibrino-hemorrhagic type of pericarditis.
  • Pericardial friction rub and possible persistent anterior chest pain.
  • Typically develops 2–3 days post-infarct and gradually resolves over the next few days.
  • Dressler Syndrome: persistence of pericarditis in post-acute MI due to formation of antibodies against damaged myocardium.
  • Severe inflammation can lead to pericardial effusion → dense fibrous adhesions → constrictive pericarditis.
Chamber Dilatation—
  • Weakening of necrotic muscles → disproportionate stretching, thinning, and dilatation of the infarcted area.
  • More common with anteroseptal forms of infarct.
Mural Thrombus, Systemic Embolism—
  • Damage to the ventricular endothelium with blood stasis, turbulence, and chamber dilatation predispose to mural thrombus.
  • Potentially leads to systemic thrombo-embolism.
Ventricular AneurysmLate complication
  • Results from large transmural and anteroseptal infarct, which heals by formation of a thin wall of scar tissue.
  • Develops months to years post-infarction.
Timing anchors for complications
  • 1st hour: greatest risk of serious arrhythmia (ventricular fibrillation).
  • 2–3 days: pericarditis develops.
  • 3–7 days: myocardial rupture (heart maximally soft).
  • Months to years: ventricular aneurysm.

Infarct Modification by Treatment p. 14

TreatmentLecture description
Thrombolysis
  • In the earliest phase, patients with MI use heparin or streptokinase to lyse the thrombus.
  • Ineffective if MI is beyond one day because thrombus has already been organized and will resist lysis.
Angioplasty & Stents
  • Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI).
  • A medical device (balloon catheter & stent) is placed on the damaged area in order to re-expand the segment of the occluded vessel.
Coronary Artery Bypass Surgery (CABG)Use of artery or vein grafts, usually from the internal thoracic artery or saphenous vein, in order to re-establish blood flow of the coronary artery.

Altered Morphology (after reperfusion)

  • Brought about by treatment in reestablishing perfusion in affected heart muscles
    • Limited coagulative necrosis: due to early restoration of blood flow
    • More contraction bands: due to hypercontraction of myocytes
    • Hemorrhage: due to leakage of blood from necrotic tissue as blood returns

Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease p. 14–15

Definition Must Know

  • Also known as "Ischemic Cardiomyopathy"
  • Progressive, congestive heart failure as a consequence of accumulated ischemic myocardial damage
  • Cardiac findings in patients, often but not exclusively elderly
  • In most instances, patients present with insidious, congestive heart failure
  • Most cases of previous myocardial infarction and history of coronary arterial interventions are elicited
  • Usually appears post-infarction due to functional decompensation of hypertrophied non-infarcted myocardium.
    • Often associated with the severe form of CA atherosclerosis
  • Account for almost 50% of cardiac transplant patients

Gross Morphology

  • Cardiomegaly, with left ventricular hypertrophy and dilatation
  • Some degree of severe stenotic CA atherosclerosis
  • Discrete scars representing healed infarcts are usually present
  • The mural endocardium often has patchy fibrous thickenings, and mural thrombus may be seen

Microscopic Findings

  • Myocardial hypertrophy
  • Diffuse subendocardial myocyte vacuolization
  • Patchy interstitial fibrosis
  • Many cardiac myocytes drop out and are replaced by scar tissue, discrete ones representing healed infarcts

Clinical Findings

  • Extensive scarring of the myocardium can compromise the contractility of patients with Chronic IHD
    • Common clinical presentation and death among these patients are progressive and intractable CHF
    • Associated multi-vessel stenosis and coronary atherosclerosis

Sudden Cardiac Death (SCD) p. 15–16

Definition Must Know

  • Sudden, unexpected death from cardiac causes that occurs either without symptoms or within 1–24 hours of symptom onset [American Heart Association]
  • Largest cause of natural death in the US
  • Most patients with SCD have some form of underlying cardiac condition: coronary artery disease, ischemic heart disease, genetic mutations associated with increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias
  • Sudden cessation of cardiac activity, producing Sudden Cardiac Arrest (SCA) → stoppage of circulation as manifested by absence of pulse and BP → organ dysfunction, tissue hypoxia, and organ failure
  • Around 80–90% of patients who had SCD: significant CA atherosclerosis, and old, healed myocardial infarct can be demonstrated

Non-atherosclerotic SCD in younger populations

  • Congenital structural or coronary arterial abnormalities
  • Aortic valve stenosis
  • Mitral valve prolapse
  • Dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
  • Myocarditis
  • Pulmonary hypertension
  • Hereditary or acquired abnormalities of the cardiac conduction system
  • Other miscellaneous causes: drugs, cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolism, systemic metabolic and hemodynamic alterations, drug abuse (cocaine and methamphetamine)

Mechanism

  • Mechanism responsible for the majority of SCD is a fatal arrhythmia, most often a ventricular fibrillation or asystole
    • Structural changes in the diseased heart as a result of inherited factors (e.g., mutations in the ion channel coding genes) cannot explain the suddenness of SCD
    • Postulations that SCD could be a consequence of electrical mechanical disjunction
    • Although ischemic injury and other cardiac conditions can affect the conduction system, most cases of fatal arrhythmias are triggered by electrical irritability of the myocardium
  • Automatic cardioverter defibrillator can sense and electrically counteract episodes of ventricular fibrillation.
    • Prognosis of patients vulnerable to SCD is markedly improved by pharmaceutical intervention.

Morphological Findings

  • 80–90% of patients: significant and severe, fixed CA atherosclerosis with critical stenosis (>75% luminal obstruction) involving single or multiple CA vessels
    • Acute plaque disruption and change is found in only 10–20% of cases
  • 40% of cases: Healed MI
  • Common feature: presence of subendocardial myocyte vacuolization indicative of severe chronic ischemia
  • SCD is increasingly seen in individuals with hypertrophic and fibrotic hearts without evidence of IHD
Key Differentiator · Chronic IHD vs SCD
  • Chronic IHD: slow, progressive and intractable CHF from accumulated scarring, "Ischemic Cardiomyopathy", ~50% of cardiac transplants.
  • SCD: sudden death within 1–24 hours from a fatal arrhythmia (ventricular fibrillation or asystole), with fixed critical stenosis (>75%) in 80–90%, acute plaque change in only 10–20%.
  • Shared finding: subendocardial myocyte vacuolization = severe chronic ischemia.

Hypertensive Heart Disease (HHD) p. 16

Definition Must Know

  • A consequence of the increased demands placed on the heart by hypertension, causing pressure overload and ventricular hypertrophy
  • A series of morphological changes in the heart and clinical consequences brought about by hypertension
TypeChamberChanges
Systemic (left-sided) HHDLeft ventricle
  • Most commonly seen.
  • Changes, thickening, and hypertrophy in the left ventricle as a result of systemic hypertension.
Pulmonary (right-sided) HHDRight ventricle
  • Also known as cor pulmonale.
  • Right ventricular dilatation: when the pulmonary hypertension is acute.
  • Right ventricular hypertrophy: when the pulmonary hypertension is long-standing and chronic.

Systemic Hypertensive Heart Disease p. 16

  • Hypertrophy of the left ventricle is an adaptive response to the pressure overload of chronic hypertension
  • Compensatory changes may be deleterious and can lead to: myocardial dysfunction, myocardial "demand" ischemia, cardiac dilation, CHF, sudden death (in some cases)
  • Complications of long-standing, left-sided HHD:
    • Progression to IHD
    • Renal damage
    • Cerebrovascular stroke
    • Progressive CHF
    • SCD
  • Patients with untreated systemic HPN may progress to systolic dysfunction and LV heart failure
  • Effective control of HPN can prevent cardiac hypertrophy and its associated complications

Diagnostic Criteria p. 16

  • Criterion 1: Presence of left ventricular hypertrophy, concentric (>2.0 cm)
    • Usually concentric in nature, in the absence of other cardiovascular pathology that may induce or explain the cardiac LV hypertrophy
  • Criterion 2: Presence of clinical history or pathologic evidence of HPN in other organs (e.g., kidney, eyes).
    • BP > 120/80 mmHg (threshold for diagnosis of HPN)
  • The Framingham Study established that even mild hypertension (>140/90 mmHg), if sufficiently prolonged, can induce left ventricular hypertrophy
  • Compensated systemic HHD may be asymptomatic, but may show ECG of left ventricular enlargement

Gross Morphology p. 16

  • Thickened LV wall (>2.0 cm) due to LV pressure overload
    • LV wall concentric thickening with a reduction in the chamber lumen
    • Associated with overall enlargement of the size and weight of the heart
    • Over time, the increased thickness of the LV wall, associated with increased interstitial connective tissue, may impart a stiffness that produces a diastolic filling problem, often leading to left atrial enlargement
    • Untreated HPN may progress to systolic dysfunction and LV heart failure

Histological Findings p. 16–17

  • Increase in the transverse diameter of the myocytes, with variable degrees of cellular and nuclear enlargement
  • Enlarged myocytes and nuclei
  • Diffuse perivascular and interstitial fibrosis of the myocardium may be seen
Clinical CueIf you see concentric LV hypertrophy >2.0 cm, papillary muscle hypertrophy, and increased size of cardiac muscle nuclei and cytoplasm in a hypertensive patient → think Systemic HHD. (Aortic stenosis is not a morphologic finding of HHD.)

Pulmonary Hypertensive Heart Disease p. 17

Definition Must Know

  • "Cor pulmonale"
  • Heart changes that mainly occur in the right ventricle in response to pressure overload in the pulmonary vasculature due to pulmonary HPN
  • Two associated morphological changes:
    • RV dilation (Acute Pulmonary HPN): acute elevation of the pulmonary pressure, like in cases with acute massive pulmonary thromboembolism, produces morphological changes of RV dilatation and RV heart failure
    • RV hypertrophy (Chronic Pulmonary HPN): chronic cor pulmonale is characterized by RV hypertrophy
  • Most of the time, pulmonary HPN occurs as a complication of left-sided heart failure
  • The right ventricle has a thinner and more compliant wall than the left ventricle because the pulmonary vasculature, normally, is the low-pressure side of the circulation
  • Isolated pulmonary HHD stems from RV pressure overload

Disorders Predisposing to Cor Pulmonale (Table 11) p. 17

TypeDiseases
Diseases of the Pulmonary Parenchyma
  • COPD
  • Diffuse pulmonary interstitial fibrosis
  • Pneumoconioses
  • Cystic fibrosis
  • Bronchiectasis
Diseases of the Pulmonary Vessels
  • Recurrent pulmonary thromboembolism
  • Primary pulmonary hypertension
  • Extensive pulmonary arteritis (e.g., Wegener granulomatosis)
  • Drug-, toxin-, or radiation-induced vascular obstruction
  • Extensive pulmonary tumor microembolism
Diseases Affecting Chest Movement
  • Kyphoscoliosis
  • Marked obesity (Pickwickian Syndrome)
  • Neuromuscular diseases
Disorders Inducing Pulmonary Arterial Constriction
  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Hypoxemia
  • Chronic altitude sickness
  • Obstruction to major airways
  • Idiopathic alveolar hypoventilation

Acute Cor Pulmonale p. 17

  • Right ventricular dilatation usually occurs after massive acute pulmonary thrombo-embolism
    • An underlying massive pulmonary embolism from the lower extremities goes up to major (L) and (R) pulmonary arteries to block them → sudden increase in pulmonary pressure is reflected in the RV
  • Gross Morphology: Marked RV dilatation without hypertrophy
    • As a result of RV dilatation, the annular ring of the tricuspid valve may be widened and dilated, resulting in tricuspid regurgitation
    • Compensatory response to the sudden elevation of pulmonary pressure.
      • The RV has no time to adapt to the pressure changes.
    • On cross-section: Normal = crescent-shaped RV chamber.
      • Pathologic = dilated globoid chamber

Chronic Cor Pulmonale p. 17

  • Right ventricular hypertrophy is caused by chronic RV pressure overload, which appears in long-standing pulmonary HPN
  • Common Causes:
    • Lung disorders, especially chronic parenchymal diseases: Emphysema, Primary pulmonary hypertension
    • COPD
    • Chronic Restrictive Pulmonary Disease (CRPD)
    • Primary intrinsic pulmonary arterial disease
    • Chest wall motion impairment
  • Gross Morphology: The RV wall becomes thick and hypertrophied
    • Sometimes up to 1.0 cm or more (Normal: 0.5 cm)
    • Caused by long-standing chronic pulmonary HPN of various causes
Key Differentiator · Acute vs Chronic Cor Pulmonale
  • Acute: massive pulmonary thromboembolism → RV dilatation without hypertrophy, globoid chamber, tricuspid regurgitation, RV has no time to adapt.
  • Chronic: long-standing pulmonary HPN (COPD, emphysema, CRPD) → RV hypertrophy, wall up to 1.0 cm or more (normal 0.5 cm).
Wall thickness anchors
  • LV normal 1.5 cm, HHD >2.0 cm.
  • RV normal 0.5 cm, chronic cor pulmonale up to 1.0 cm or more.

  • Cell and mitochondrial swelling within minutes

Red-Exclamation Must-Knows (lecture wording)

Must Know
  • TIP: All of the letter Ts in CHD = Right to Left Shunt anomalies.
  • Ischemic episodes in angina pectoris DO NOT produce irreversible cell death.
  • TAKE NOTE: Pattern of progression of necrosis advances in a wavefront manner.
  • Table 6: salient morphological changes at different time intervals following infarction (see grid below).
  • Irreversible cell injury: 20–40 minutes. Medical intervention should be instituted before this time to prevent irreversible cell death.
  • Aerobic metabolism ceases within seconds (early biochemical change).
  • Sarcolemmal membrane damage = earliest detectable feature of myocyte necrosis (early ultrastructural change).
  • TTC: Viable myocardium = pink to red.
    • Non-viable = yellow.

Core Definitions

  • IHD ("Coronary Heart Disease", "Coronary Artery Disease"): group of related cardiac diseases from imbalance between blood supply (perfusion) and demand for oxygen. >90% due to obstructive coronary artery atherosclerotic lesions.
  • Angina Pectoris: paroxysmal, recurrent precordial or substernal chest pain from transient myocardial ischemia which falls short of infarction (15 seconds to minutes).
    • Insufficient to induce myocardial necrosis.
  • Myocardial Infarction ("heart attack"): localized area of cardiac muscle necrosis due to ischemia.
    • Irreversible necrosis secondary to prolonged ischemia, usually CA atherosclerosis with plaque rupture and superimposed occlusive thrombus.
  • Acute Coronary Syndrome: spectrum of unstable angina, AMI, SCD from sudden reduced coronary blood flow after conversion of a stable plaque to an unstable atherothrombotic lesion.
  • Chronic IHD ("Ischemic Cardiomyopathy"): progressive CHF from accumulated ischemic myocardial damage.
  • Sudden Cardiac Death: sudden unexpected death from cardiac causes, without symptoms or within 1–24 hours of symptom onset.
    • Mechanism: fatal arrhythmia (ventricular fibrillation or asystole).
  • HHD: increased demands by hypertension → pressure overload and ventricular hypertrophy.
    • Systemic (LV) vs Pulmonary (RV, cor pulmonale).

Mechanisms

Sequence of coronary artery thrombosis

1 Fixed plaque → acute plaque change (fissure, ulcer, hemorrhage)→2 Platelets adhere, aggregate → primary hemostatic plug + vasospasm (thromboxane, ADP, serotonin)→3 Tissue factor activates coagulation (extrinsic + intrinsic)→4 Thrombus propagates → occludes lumen → infarction

Wavefront necrosis

Starts subendocardial (least perfused, high intramural pressure)→spreads outward in a wavefront→driven by tissue edema, ROS, inflammatory mediators→full thickness by 24 hr

The 5 IHD mechanisms

  • Fixed obstruction: stable plaque, thick fibrous cap, 90% of narrowing, collaterals form → typical angina
  • Acute plaque change: rupture, fissuring, superficial erosion, ulceration, hemorrhage → ACS
  • Thrombosis: complete → transmural MI.
    • Partial → unstable angina, subendocardial MI, SCD
  • Vasoconstriction: adrenergic agents, platelet factors, endothelin.
    • Reduces flow and raises plaque rupture risk
  • Inflammation: T cells, macrophages, TNF, IL-6, IFN-gamma, metalloproteinase later.
    • Marker: CRP

Non-atheromatous occlusion (<10%)

  • CA embolism (cholesterol), dissecting aneurysm (aortic root → coronary ostia), vasospasm, congenital anomalies, trauma, vasculitis (Kawasaki's)

Diagnostic Anchors

  • 3 parameters for AMI: classical S/S + ECG (ST elevation, new Q waves) + markers (CPK-MB, troponin I & T, CK, LDH, CRP)
  • Excludes MI: no change in CK and CK-MB in first 2 days and no troponin change in the days following
  • Troponin = most clinically useful (high sensitivity and specificity).
    • Significant elevation also in myocarditis, myocardial trauma.
    • "Troponin leak" (low levels) in CHF, PE, sepsis, resuscitation
  • CK isomers: BB brain, MB heart (intermediate), MM skeletal (slowest)
  • LDH lacks specificity (shock, RBC hemolysis, carcinomatosis)
  • STEMI = transmural = complete occlusion.
    • NSTEMI = subendocardial = partial occlusion
  • Systemic HHD criteria: (1) concentric LVH >2.0 cm without other explanation, (2) history or evidence of HPN in other organs (kidney, eyes), BP >120/80
  • Atypical MI: diabetics (asymptomatic, neuropathy), women (lesser, neck, back, epigastric pain)

Complications Timeline

1st hour: serious arrhythmia (VF)→2–3 days: fibrino-hemorrhagic pericarditis→3–7 days: rupture (heart maximally soft) → hemopericardium, tamponade→Months–years: ventricular aneurysm
  • Most frequent: contractile dysfunction 60% (HF 60%, cardiogenic shock 10% when ≥40% LV damaged).
    • LVF → hypotension, pulmonary edema, congestion
  • Rupture (1–5%, fatal): LV free wall most common → tamponade.
    • Septum → acquired VSD, L→R shunt.
    • Papillary muscle → mitral regurgitation
  • Arrhythmia: septal infarcts, 90% develop rhythm disturbance, heart block, tachyarrhythmia, asystole, bradycardia, PVCs
  • Dressler Syndrome: persistent pericarditis, antibodies against damaged myocardium.
    • Effusion → adhesions → constrictive pericarditis
  • Anteroseptal infarcts → chamber dilatation, ventricular aneurysm (thin scar wall)
  • Mural thrombus (endothelial damage, stasis, turbulence, dilatation) → systemic embolism
  • RCA occlusion → RV infarction (1–3%), posterior septal infarction, right sided HF
  • LAD occlusion → septum → potentially fatal arrhythmia.
    • LCX or LAD main branch → wider infarct

Treatment Anchors

  • Thrombolysis (heparin, streptokinase): earliest phase only.
    • Ineffective beyond one day (thrombus organized)
  • PCI: balloon catheter & stent re-expand the occluded segment
  • CABG: internal thoracic artery or saphenous vein grafts
  • Reperfusion morphology: limited coagulative necrosis, more contraction bands, hemorrhage

If You See X → Think Y

Clinical Cues
  • Exertional chest pain <15 min relieved by rest → Stable angina.
  • Chest pain at rest, young patient, transient ST elevation, relieved by nitroglycerin → Prinzmetal angina.
  • Crescendo pain >20 min, new onset, at rest → Unstable angina (pre-infarction).
  • Crushing pain >30 min, ST elevation, raised troponin, no relief with nitroglycerin → AMI (STEMI).
  • Wavy thinned fibers, no neutrophils → AMI ½–4 hours.
  • Tiger stripe papillary muscles, neutrophils → AMI 1–3 days.
  • Central softening, hyperemic border, macrophages → AMI 3–7 days, rupture risk.
  • Red-gray depressed center, granulation tissue → AMI 10–14 days.
  • Gray-white scar, hyalinized collagen → AMI 2–8 weeks.
  • Pale yellow unstained area on TTC → non-viable infarct.
  • Pericardial friction rub 2–3 days post-MI → fibrino-hemorrhagic pericarditis.
    • Persistent → Dressler Syndrome.
  • Hemopericardium 3–7 days post-MI → LV free wall rupture.
  • Concentric LV >2.0 cm + hypertension → Systemic HHD.
  • RV as thick as LV + COPD/smoking, no CAD or valve disease → Chronic cor pulmonale (pulmonary HPN).
  • Dilated globoid RV after massive PE → Acute cor pulmonale.
  • Subendocardial myocyte vacuolization → severe chronic ischemia (chronic IHD, SCD).

Common Confusions and Exam Traps

Exam Traps
  • Angina = no irreversible cell death.
    • MI = coagulative necrosis.
  • Most common precipitating event of AMI = acute plaque disruption/change, and the most frequent cause of occlusion = thrombosis on top of atherosclerosis.
  • Transmural ≠ "most common" — but STEMI is the more serious form.
    • Subendocardial occurs without acute plaque change.
  • TTC stains viable tissue (pink-red).
    • The infarct is the yellow unstained area.
  • Earliest biochemical change = aerobic metabolism ceases (seconds).
    • Earliest ultrastructural = sarcolemmal damage.
    • Earliest light microscopic = wavy fibers.
    • Gross visible only at 12–24 hr.
  • Rupture happens at 3–7 days (maximally soft), not immediately.
  • Troponin, not CK-MB, is the most clinically useful marker.
    • LDH normalizes last (8–14 days).
  • Thrombolysis is ineffective beyond one day.
  • Systemic HHD = LV, concentric.
    • Aortic stenosis is not a morphologic finding of HHD.
  • Acute pulmonary HPN = RV dilatation.
    • Chronic = RV hypertrophy.
  • Secundum ASD (90%) is at the fossa ovale.
    • Primum = near AV valve + cleft mitral.
    • Sinus venosus = near SVC + TAPVR.

Study Aid (not lecture statements)

Study aid · cell sequence in a healing infarct Neutrophils (1–3 d) → Macrophages (3–7 d) → Granulation tissue (7–14 d) → Scar (2–8 wk, complete >2 mo). "N-M-G-S" follows the lecture's own Table 6 order.
